job.style: a passage rich in numbers, dates or measurements

passage: The pre-modern world was far more interconnected than many assume, with trade routes spanning vast distances long before the modern era. The Silk Routes, which flourished from the 2nd century BCE, were not merely for silk; they facilitated the exchange of gold, spices, textiles, and even religions like Buddhism. By the 16th century, the Columbian Exchange introduced crops like potatoes, chilies, and maize to Europe and India, items previously unknown in these regions. European dominance in the Americas was not solely due to weaponry, but largely driven by the accidental introduction of smallpox, which decimated local populations. In the 1890s, the cattle plague known as rinderpest devastated Africa, killing 90 percent of the continent's livestock and destroying the traditional livelihoods of local communities. Later, the 1944 Bretton Woods Conference established the IMF and World Bank, institutions designed to manage global financial stability rather than specifically aiding developing nations. By the 1960s, the G-77 was formed by developing countries to demand a New International Economic Order, seeking a fairer share of global wealth against the dominance of the world's wealthiest economies.

items.evidence: The Silk Routes, which flourished from the 2nd century BCE, were not merely for silk; they facilitated the exchange of gold, spices, textiles, and even religions like Buddhism.
items.q: Why is the name 'Silk Routes' only part of the story?
options: Many other goods and beliefs also travelled them
They were one road built for silk alone
They linked only nearby lands, not distant ones
They began only in the modern era
items.explain: The Silk Routes also carried gold, spices, textiles and religions like Buddhism, not just silk.

wrong.why: thinks it was a single road only for silk
thinks old trade was only between neighbours
thinks global links are only modern

items.evidence: By the 16th century, the Columbian Exchange introduced crops like potatoes, chilies, and maize to Europe and India, items previously unknown in these regions.
items.q: Why would chilies in an Indian dish from 1300 be a historical mistake?
options: Chilies reached India only in the 16th century
Chilies grew in India but were costly then
Chilies were carried to Europe, but not India
Chilies went from India to the Americas later
items.explain: The Columbian Exchange brought chilies to India in the 16th century; before that they were unknown there.

wrong.why: thinks chilies were always in Indian food
misses that India is named with Europe
reverses the direction of the exchange

items.evidence: European dominance in the Americas was not solely due to weaponry, but largely driven by the accidental introduction of smallpox, which decimated local populations.
items.q: Local populations in the Americas collapsed after Europeans arrived. What was the main cause?
options: A disease the Europeans spread by accident
The guns and cannons used in battles
A cattle plague that killed their animals
A shortage of food crops like maize
items.explain: Smallpox, brought accidentally by Europeans, killed huge numbers of local people; weapons were not the main reason.

wrong.why: thinks superior weapons won the Americas
mixes smallpox up with rinderpest in Africa
grabs a crop named nearby as a cause

items.evidence: In the 1890s, the cattle plague known as rinderpest devastated Africa, killing 90 percent of the continent's livestock and destroying the traditional livelihoods of local communities.
items.q: How did rinderpest harm African communities in the 1890s?
options: It wiped out their cattle and their income
It killed millions of African people directly
It spread smallpox through their villages
It destroyed their crops of maize and potatoes
items.explain: Rinderpest killed 90 percent of Africa's livestock, so people lost the cattle they lived on.

wrong.why: mixes it up with smallpox in the Americas
